constraints.name: The decision rests on unstructured interviews and gut judgement
The first screen rejects qualified people on proxies
The selection criteria have never been validated or documented
Slow decisions and slow offers lose candidates
A long, repetitive or opaque process drives withdrawal
The technical interview measures anxiety as much as skill
The most valid tests show the largest group differences
An automated or AI screen carries liability and notice duties the firm has not met
The firm asks for what the law reserves until after a conditional offer
Too few qualified candidates within reach
The posting draws volume without fit
The firm cannot tell which channel produces hires who stay
The referral network is narrow and reproduces itself
Candidates do not know the firm, or know it unfavourably
The ad's words and its delivery exclude people the firm wants
A degree or years-of-experience requirement shrinks the pool for little validity
The cleared pool is closed and expensive
The salary the market expects exceeds what the contract rate can carry
Contract rates escalate slower than the labor market
Larger employers offer more total compensation than the salary comparison shows
A market-rate offer puts the new hire above the people already doing the job
The way the offer is made creates legal exposure or a gap the firm did not intend
Accepted candidates withdraw or take a counteroffer before they start
The offer depends on an award the firm does not control
The firm can sponsor a clearance only for a contract it already has
The clearance takes longer than the opening can wait
Eligibility is not access to the site, the network or the program
The longer the wait between acceptance and start, the more accepted hires never start
Payroll before access is the firm's cost, not the customer's
The first three days carry statutory clocks the firm cannot move
A foreign national cannot start on controlled or classified work without an authorization
Adjustment is left to the newcomer
The ramp to full productivity is longer than the rate assumes
The customer will not accept, or pay for, a junior in the slot
The skills the firm pays for are portable
Mentoring capacity is the senior staff's billable time
Training that does not look like the work does not transfer
Development runs ahead of a place to use it
The return on development is not measured, so every departure looks like failure
Pay falls behind what the person can do and what the person next to them gets
A small firm has few steps up, and the obvious step is the wrong one
The employee is run by the customer and forgotten by the firm
One vacancy loads the rest, and the load shows up as stress, not hours
An onsite, fixed-schedule job competes against arrangements it cannot offer
The job ends when the contract does, and the person knows it
The prime, the customer or a competitor hires the person the firm trained
The knowledge the contract depends on sits with one or two people
A departure sets contract and security clocks running
An internal move keeps the person and opens a new vacancy with the whole clock
The opening is tentative, unfunded or staffed for a proposal
The requisition describes several jobs as one
Preferences are written as requirements, and nobody can say whose they are
The firm and the customer mean different things by "qualified"
The customer's approval has no clock and the candidate does
Recruiting spend is visible, vacancy cost and cash exposure are not
Some roles cannot be staffed profitably at the contract's rate
Recruiting starts when the vacancy opens, and every vacancy is treated alike
Partner support is capped, consented and competitively constrained
Staffing decisions run on anecdote because the records are not kept
Nobody owns the requisition from opening to start
